The four important properties of singularities in the minimal model program are ter- minal, canonical, log terminal, and log canonical. There are the following implications among them: terminal ⇒ canonical ⇒ log terminal ⇒ log canonical Tame quotient singularities are always log terminal. Wild quotient singularities are sometimes log terminal, but sometimes they are not. It is desirable to have useful criteria to decide whether the given wild quotient singularity is log terminal or not. needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 3.2. Find a purely representation-theoretic criterion for whether Adk /G is log terminal (resp. terminal, canonical, log canonical). Note that for terminal and canonical singularities, the problem makes sense in the tame case as well. The criterion in this case is known as the Reid–Shepherd-Barron–Tai criterion (e.g., see [Yas06, Cor. 6]), which uses ages of g ∈ G\{1}, invariants determined by eigenvalues. In the wild case, we have R a criterion for each of the above four classes of singularities in terms of the integral ∆G Ld−v in (2.6) (see [Yas20, Cor 1.4]). However, to compute this integral, we have to compute the moduli space ∆G and the function v on it, which is generally complex and not representation-theoretic. When G = Z/pn Z, we have an affirmative answer to the problem [Yas14b, Yas19, TY20a, Tan21]. Yamamoto [Yam21a] proved that the quotient variety A3k /(Z/3Z)2 in characteristic three is not log canonical, provided that the group has no pseudo-reflection. However, from any proper subgroup G ( (Z/3Z)2 , based on [Yas14b], the quotient A3k /G is canonical. This example shows that we cannot reduce the problem to the case of cyclic groups by restricting the given representation to cyclic subgroups. Problem 3.1 would be much harder when G non-linearly acts on a smooth variety and when G acts on a singular variety. Note that the tame action on a smooth variety is always locally linearizable; each point x ∈ X has local coordinates for which the action of the stabilizer is linear. This is no longer the case for the wild action. Perhaps we should start with the actions of Z/p on Spec kJx, yK fixing only the closed point. This action is never linear. needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 4.1. When does there exist a crepant resolution of Adk /G? Is it possible to construct a crepant resolution as a certain moduli space? The McKay correspondence, (2.4) and (2.6), takes the simplest form when there exists a crepant resolution Y → Adk /G, owing to (2.3). We would like to know when this is the case. In characteristic zero, for a finite subgroup G ⊂ SLd (C) with d ≤ 3, there exists a crepant resolution of AdC /G. In dimension two, the minimal resolution is a crepant resolution. In dimension three, this was proved via a case-by-case analysis by Roan, Ito, and Markushevich (see [Roa96] and references therein). It was later proved in [Nak01, BKR01] that the G-Hilbert scheme becomes a crepant resolution in this case, thereby giving a moduli-theoretic construction of a crepant resolution. For the wild case, the following is a list of all the examples that the author knows: (1) The symmetric product of an affine plane A2n n 2 k /Sn = S Ak in any characteristic; n the Hilbert scheme of n points on A2k , Hilb (A2k ), gives a crepant resolution [KT01, BK05]. (2) A quotient of A2n k by the wreath product (Z/2Z) ≀ Sn in characteristic 6= 2, as in [WY17].

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 5.1. Suppose that Mst (Adk /G) 6= ∞. Is Mst (Adk /G) a rational function in L1/♯G ? In the tame case, from Equation (2.6), Mst (Adk /G) is the sum of powers of L1/♯G , in particular, a polynomial in L1/♯G . In the wild case, it is not necessarily a polynomial (see computation in [Yas14b]). However, to the best of the author’s knowledge, it is always a rational function. Remark 5.2. Even in the tame case, if k is not algebraically closed, then Mst (Adk /G) is generally not a rational function in L1/♯G (cf. [WY15, Th. 5.9 and Cor. 5.11]). However, a weaker rationality as in the next problem holds over any field in the tame case.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 7.2. Is the v-function upper-semicontinuous? To make this problem precise, we first need to decide what geometric structure to give to the moduli space ∆G . Thus, the problem is related to the construction of this moduli space, which we discuss in the next section. The w-function mentioned above is used in the following variant of the wild McKay correspondence: Z Mst (Adk /G)o = Lw ∆G Cf. Section 6. This version is not explicitly stated in the literature, but its point- counting version appears in [Yas17b]. We can prove the above equality by combining arguments of [Yas17b] and the proof of (2.6) in [Yas20]. In the above equality, we need to use the definition of w in [Yas17b], which is slightly different from the original one in [Yas17a, WY15]. The two definitions coincide for a few important cases (see [Yas17b, Rem. 8.2 and Lem. 8.3]). However, no example in which they are, indeed, different functions has been found so far.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Problem 14.2. Consider a tower X ← Y1 ← Y2 ← · · · of Galois quasi-étale coverings as above and let yi ∈ Yi and Gi be the point and Galois group as above for the Galois covering Yi → X. Does the sequence Mst (Y1 )y1 /G1 ≥ Mst (Y2 )y1 /G2 ≥ · · · satisfy the descending chain condition (DCC)? In the paper mentioned above, it is proved that the answer to this problem is also affirmative in dimension two. By combining it with the strictness of inequality, it can be observed that the local étale fundamental group of a log-terminal surface singularity is finite (in any characteristic).
